newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sees little impact from CME futures plan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sees little impact from CME futures plan.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange's plan to list Taiwan stock index futures on its GLOBEX system will not hinder the island's drive to launch its own futures market, local regulators said on Thursday.
The CME said on Wednesday its board had approved plans to offer Taiwan futures and options based on the Dow Jones Stock Exchange Index -- the first derivatives linked to Taiwan stocks.
The contracts would be listed initially on the CME's 24-hour worldwide GLOBEX trading system. No target date was given.
The CME's move puts new pressure on Taiwan's Securities and Exchange Commission, which is overseeing development of Taiwan's first futures exchange and has vowed to start trading in July.

Taiwan bans trade in unapproved financial products, but the CME system, even if not authorised by Taipei, could give local investors unprecedented access to Taiwan index futures during the Taiwan trading day -- assuming local brokerages were willing to pass investor orders to offshore branches.
Commission officials said the CME/GLOBEX move would not influence planning for Taiwan's exchange.

"The CME's product still needs formal approval from the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission and it will not change our decision to establish Taiwan's own futures exchange," commission official Lo Chin-an told Reuters by telephone.
Taiwan has no known plans to approve the CME products.

Developers of Taiwan's exchange, working under a cooperation pact with the Chicago Board of Trade -- the CME's arch rival -- face one more big hurdle, the need for parliament's passage of a draft Futures Exchange and Trading Law.
The draft has passed committee and is expected to be enacted by the full Legislative Yuan by early 1997, providing a legal basis for trading, Lo said.

Local futures brokers welcomed the CME's apparent early start in the race to launch Taiwan index futures and said any early advantage gained by the CME could be lost once Taiwan's operation gets started, due mainly to time differences.
"It would be easier to monitor a market that opens and closes at the same time as the stock exchange," a broker said.
Brokers said most trading volume likely would come from local customers for simple reasons of proximity and convenience, especially during Taiwan's Saturday trading session.
